project_title: ISL-Speak: Indian Sign Language Gesture-to-Speech System

author_context.student: Kesav, B.E. CSE (AI & ML), Chennai Institute of Technology
author_context.ide: Google Antigravity IDE (local agentic dev environment)
author_context.instructions_for_agent: This entire JSON is a single master instruction set. Read it top to bottom before writing any code. Execute phases sequentially. Never attempt model training inside Antigravity/local machine — every training step must produce a Colab-ready .ipynb notebook or script pushed to Drive/GitHub instead. Local machine is only for: repo scaffolding, data preprocessing scripts (light, non-GPU), Flask/Streamlit inference app, TTS integration, and documentation.

problem_statement: Build a system that takes a video of a person performing an Indian Sign Language (ISL) gesture, classifies the gesture into a word/phrase using a CNN+LSTM/Transformer pipeline, and converts the recognized word sequence into audible speech via TTS — enabling real-time accessibility for the Indian deaf and hard-of-hearing community. ASL has many mature open-source projects; ISL is comparatively underexplored, which is the core novelty and impact angle for this project.

primary.name: INCLUDE: Indian Sign Language Dataset
primary.source_org: AI4Bharat, IIT Madras (recorded with St. Louis School for the Deaf, Adyar, Chennai)
primary.size: 4292 videos total (paper cites 4287; 5 added later) — 3475 in train.csv, 817 in test.csv
primary.classes: ~263 word/sign classes across categories like Greetings, Colours, Society, Electronics, etc.
primary.access: Hosted via AI4Bharat OpenHands project; search 'AI4Bharat INCLUDE dataset download' — dataset is distributed as per-category zip files of short video clips
primary.notes: Full INCLUDE is large (many GB of video). For a hackathon/course-project timeline, start with the INCLUDE-50 subset (50 words, 25 videos each) to get an end-to-end pipeline working fast, then scale to more classes if time allows.

fallback.name: INCLUDE-50
fallback.why: Smaller, faster to download and iterate on Colab free-tier without hitting disk/RAM limits.

dataset.licensing_note: Confirm the dataset's license/terms of use before redistribution; cite the INCLUDE paper (Sridhar et al.) in the final report.

pipeline: 2. Frame extraction + landmark extraction using MediaPipe Holistic (pose + both hands + face mesh subset)
3. Sequence of keypoint vectors per video (NOT raw pixels — this is the key design decision, see rationale below)
4. Temporal model: LSTM / BiLSTM / small Transformer encoder classifies the keypoint sequence into a gesture/word class
5. Predicted word(s) assembled into a sentence (simple grammar smoothing / word buffer)
6. Text-to-Speech (TTS) engine converts the sentence to audio output
high_level_architecture.design_rationale_keypoints_over_raw_vide: Training a 3D-CNN or CNN+LSTM directly on raw video frames is heavy (large tensors, slow, GPU-memory hungry) and hard to justify running repeatedly on Colab free tier within hackathon time. Extracting MediaPipe pose/hand landmarks first reduces each frame to a small numeric vector (~150-225 floats), so the temporal model trains on lightweight sequences (frames x features) instead of (frames x H x W x 3) video tensors. This is faster to train, smaller to store, and still captures the motion dynamics that matter for sign recognition. State this explicitly in the report as an engineering decision, not a limitation.
high_level_architecture.alternative_if_time_permits: Once the keypoint-based LSTM baseline works end-to-end, optionally add a CNN branch (e.g., MobileNetV2 features from cropped hand regions) fused with the keypoint LSTM for a hybrid model — this becomes the 'stretch goal' / novelty upgrade if the base pipeline is done early.

phases.title: Landmark Extraction Pipeline (MediaPipe)
phases.goal: Convert raw videos into fixed-format numeric keypoint sequences — this is the single most important preprocessing step and determines model input shape for the rest of the project.
steps: Write src/preprocessing/extract_landmarks.py using MediaPipe Holistic to extract per-frame landmarks: pose (33 points), left hand (21 points), right hand (21 points). Optionally include a reduced face mesh subset for mouth-shape cues, but pose+hands is sufficient for a first version.

For each frame, flatten (x, y, [z], visibility) for each landmark into a single vector. Decide and document a fixed feature-vector length (e.g., pose 33*4 + left hand 21*3 + right hand 21*3 = 264 features/frame as an example — compute your actual number and keep it consistent everywhere).
Handle variable video length: define a fixed sequence length (e.g., 40-60 frames). Uniformly sample or pad/truncate every video to this length so all training examples have the same shape (T, F).
Handle missing-landmark frames (e.g., hand out of view): fill with zeros or the previous frame's values (documented choice), don't silently crash.
Save each processed video as a .npy file named by video_id in data/landmarks/, plus a labels.csv mapping video_id -> class label -> numeric class index.

This script should be runnable BOTH locally (for the small sample, to verify correctness) AND as a Colab cell (for the full dataset, using GPU-accelerated video decode if available, though MediaPipe itself is CPU-based).
Test on the small local sample first: confirm output shape is exactly (T, F) for every processed video before scaling up on Colab.
phases.antigravity_agent_prompt: Write src/preprocessing/extract_landmarks.py. Use MediaPipe Holistic to process a folder of ISL sign videos. For each video: read frames with OpenCV, run MediaPipe Holistic on each frame to extract pose landmarks (33 points x 4 values: x,y,z,visibility), left hand landmarks (21 points x 3 values: x,y,z), and right hand landmarks (21 points x 3 values: x,y,z), concatenate them into one feature vector per frame, and if a hand/pose is not detected in a frame fill that segment with zeros. Uniformly sample or pad each video's frame sequence to a fixed length of 45 frames (configurable constant SEQ_LEN). Save the resulting (SEQ_LEN, num_features) array as a .npy file per video into data/landmarks/, and append a row (video_id, label, npy_path) to data/splits/labels.csv. Include a __main__ block that processes all videos in a given input folder and prints progress with tqdm. Add clear docstrings and a comment explaining the exact feature vector length calculation.
acceptance_criteria: Every .npy file has identical shape (SEQ_LEN, num_features)
labels.csv correctly maps video_id to class
Script handles at least one video with a missing hand landmark without crashing
Runs successfully on the small local sample

phases.title: Model Architecture Design
phases.goal: Design the sequence classifier that maps a (SEQ_LEN, num_features) keypoint sequence to a gesture/word class.
steps: Baseline model: a 2-layer BiLSTM over the keypoint sequence, followed by a dense classification head with dropout and softmax over num_classes. This is the primary deliverable model — get this working first.

Stretch model: a small Transformer encoder (2-4 layers, 4-8 attention heads) over the same input, with a learned positional encoding and a classification token or mean-pooling head. Compare against the LSTM baseline.

Write both as separate, swappable modules in src/models/ (lstm_classifier.py, transformer_classifier.py) sharing a common interface (forward(x) -> logits) so the training script can select either via a config flag.
Keep model sizes modest — this must train quickly on Colab's free-tier GPU (T4). A BiLSTM with hidden_size=128-256 and a 2-4 layer Transformer with d_model=128-256 are both appropriately sized.
Add class-weighted loss (nn.CrossEntropyLoss(weight=...)) if class imbalance was noted in Phase 1.
phases.antigravity_agent_prompt: Write two PyTorch model files. First, src/models/lstm_classifier.py: a class SignLSTMClassifier(nn.Module) with a bidirectional 2-layer LSTM (input_size=num_features, hidden_size=128, batch_first=True), followed by dropout(0.3), a linear layer from hidden_size*2 to num_classes, using the final hidden state (concatenated forward+backward) for classification. Second, src/models/transformer_classifier.py: a class SignTransformerClassifier(nn.Module) with a linear input projection to d_model=128, learned positional embeddings for SEQ_LEN positions, a nn.TransformerEncoder with 3 layers and 4 heads, mean-pooling over the sequence dimension, then a linear classification head to num_classes. Both classes should take (num_features, num_classes, seq_len) as constructor arguments and expose a forward(x) method where x has shape (batch, seq_len, num_features), returning logits of shape (batch, num_classes). Include short docstrings explaining the architecture choice.
acceptance_criteria: Both models instantiate without error given dummy input of the correct shape
Forward pass produces logits of shape (batch, num_classes)
Models share a consistent constructor interface

phases.title: Colab Training Notebook (GPU) — THE CORE TRAINING STEP

steps: In Colab: Runtime -> Change runtime type -> GPU (T4 is sufficient). Mount Drive and load the packaged X_train/y_train/... .npz files from Phase 3.
Clone the GitHub repo into Colab (or pip install -e . / sys.path append) so src/models/*.py can be imported directly — avoid duplicating model code inside the notebook.

Write the training loop in notebooks/03_model_training.ipynb: standard PyTorch loop with CrossEntropyLoss, Adam optimizer (lr=1e-3 with a scheduler like ReduceLROnPlateau or CosineAnnealingLR), track train/val loss and accuracy per epoch, save the best model checkpoint (by val accuracy) to Drive after every improvement.

Write src/inference/sentence_buffer.py: a simple buffer that accumulates consecutive predicted words, applies basic smoothing (e.g., require the same prediction for N consecutive frames/windows before accepting it, to avoid flickering predictions triggering speech every frame), and flushes to speech after a pause or a fixed word count.
Unit test the TTS module standalone (feed it a hardcoded list of words like ['hello', 'thank', 'you'] and confirm audio plays).

cross_cutting_reminders_for_agent: NEVER attempt to train the LSTM/Transformer model inside the Antigravity local environment — always generate/edit Colab notebook code and instruct the user to run it in the Colab browser tab.

Keep the feature-vector length and SEQ_LEN constants defined in exactly ONE shared config location (e.g., src/preprocessing/config.py) and import them everywhere (extraction, training, inference) to avoid shape mismatches between training and real-time inference.
Every time a model architecture changes, retrain on Colab — do not assume old checkpoints are compatible.
Keep raw video and extracted landmark arrays out of git; only track code, small metadata CSVs/JSONs, and final trained checkpoints via Git LFS or a Drive link in the README.

Prioritize getting phases 0-8 working end-to-end on a SMALL subset (e.g., 10-15 classes) before scaling to the full class list — a working small demo beats an incomplete large one, especially under hackathon/coursework deadlines.

Log any deviation from this plan (e.g., switching TensorFlow instead of PyTorch, changing SEQ_LEN) directly in README.md's 'Design Decisions' section so the final report stays consistent with the actual code.
novelty_and_presentation_talking_points: ASL (American Sign Language) has dozens of mature open-source recognition projects and large well-known datasets; ISL has comparatively few deep-learning-based public projects despite India having one of the world's largest deaf populations — this is a genuine, citable accessibility gap.

Using MediaPipe keypoint sequences instead of raw video is a deliberate engineering trade-off for feasibility under Colab-free-tier / hackathon time constraints — frame this as efficient design, not a shortcut.

The end-to-end gesture-to-SPEECH (not just gesture-to-text) framing directly targets real-world accessibility: it lets a deaf signer 'speak' to someone who doesn't know sign language, which is the actual use case that matters.
